analogy.p: The genome is like a huge cookery library kept in the nucleus. Each chromosome is one volume, each gene is a single recipe, and each triplet is a three-letter word that tells the cook which ingredient (amino acid) to add next. The order of the words matters: change the order and you get a different dish (protein). The twisted ladder is like a book printed twice in mirror image, so a damaged page can always be rebuilt from its partner. The analogy breaks down because a cook reads a recipe once, whereas the cell reads genes repeatedly, and a recipe book has no way to copy itself.

bullets: DNA is a **polymer**: a very long molecule made of many small repeating units joined in a chain.
The repeating units are called **nucleotides**.
DNA is made of **two strands** that are coiled together to form a **double helix** (a twisted ladder shape).
In eukaryotic cells (animals and plants) DNA is inside the **nucleus**; in a human body cell it is split into **23 pairs of chromosomes** (46 in total).
The code is stored in the **order of the bases** along the strands, in the same way that the order of letters stores meaning in a sentence.
DNA is the genetic material that is **copied and passed on** to daughter cells when cells divide, and to offspring through gametes.
core.h: What DNA is and where it is found
core.p: **DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the molecule that carries the **genetic information** of living things. In plant and animal cells it is found in the **nucleus**, packaged into structures called **chromosomes**. The information in DNA is a code that tells the cell which **proteins** to make, and because proteins control the chemical reactions and structures of a cell, DNA ultimately controls how an organism develops and functions.

bullets: **Nucleus**: the organelle that contains the genetic material in the form of chromosomes.
**Chromosome**: a long, coiled molecule of DNA. Each chromosome carries **many genes**.
**Gene**: a small section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a **particular sequence of amino acids**, to make a specific protein.
**Base triplet**: a group of three bases in a row that codes for one amino acid.
**Genome**: all of the genetic material in an organism (all the genes and other DNA).
A useful order to remember (biggest to smallest): **cell, nucleus, chromosome, gene, triplet, base**.
core.h: From cell to gene: the levels of organisation
core.p: Students must be able to link the levels from the cell down to the individual gene. A cell contains a nucleus; the nucleus contains chromosomes; each chromosome is one very long molecule of DNA; and a small section of that DNA that codes for one protein is a gene. Seeing the hierarchy clearly stops you mixing up the words, which is a very common source of lost marks.

bullets: DNA is a polymer made up of **two strands** forming a **double helix**.
Each strand is a chain of nucleotides joined by their sugar and phosphate parts.
The two strands are held together by **hydrogen bonds** between bases, which are individually **weak**.
The weak bonds matter because the strands can be **separated (unzipped)** when DNA is copied or when a gene is read, then pair up again.
The many hydrogen bonds along the whole length make the molecule overall **stable**.
The helix shape packs a very long molecule into a tiny nucleus.
core.h: DNA as a polymer: the double helix
core.p: A polymer is a long molecule built by joining many smaller units (monomers) end to end. In DNA the monomers are nucleotides. Two long polymer strands run alongside each other and are held together by bonds between their bases. The pair of strands twists into a spiral, which is why the structure is called a **double helix**. Chemically it behaves like a twisted ladder: the sides are the two backbones and the rungs are pairs of bases.

bullets: Nucleotide = **common sugar + phosphate group + one of four bases**.
The sugar in DNA is deoxyribose, which is why it is called **deoxyribo**nucleic acid; at GCSE you only need to call it the sugar.
**Alternating sugar and phosphate groups** in each strand form the **sugar-phosphate backbone**.
The backbone is the same all along the molecule, so it carries no code; the **bases** carry the code.
Each sugar is attached to one base, which projects inwards towards the other strand.
The nucleotides in one strand are all joined in a single line, giving DNA its long, thread-like shape.
core.p: Every **nucleotide** has three parts: a **common sugar**, a **phosphate group**, and **one base**. The sugar of one nucleotide joins to the phosphate of the next nucleotide, so the strand has a repeating pattern of sugar, phosphate, sugar, phosphate. This alternating chain is called the **sugar-phosphate backbone** and it forms the outside edge of the ladder. The base of each nucleotide sticks inwards and is the only part that differs between nucleotides.

bullets: **A** = adenine, **T** = thymine, **C** = cytosine, **G** = guanine.
The sequence of bases along a strand is the genetic code, like a four-letter alphabet.
Different genes have different sequences, and different organisms have different genomes.
Even though there are only four letters, a long sequence can store enormous amounts of information (a human genome is about **3 billion base pairs**).
Thymine (T) is found in DNA; do not write that DNA contains uracil (that is RNA, beyond GCSE).
Examiners often show a sequence of bases and ask you to write the complementary strand, so learn the pairing rule perfectly.
core.p: There are only **four different bases** in DNA, and each is represented by a letter: **A** (adenine), **T** (thymine), **C** (cytosine) and **G** (guanine). You only need the letters A, T, C and G for the exam, though knowing the names is a bonus. Because the backbone never changes, the information in DNA is carried entirely by the **order (sequence) of these four bases**.

bullets: **A pairs with T** (two hydrogen bonds); **C pairs with G** (three hydrogen bonds).
The strands are **complementary**: the sequence on one strand determines the sequence on the other.
Example: strand ATGC pairs with strand TACG.
In any double-stranded DNA, the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of C equals the amount of G.
This rule lets you do percentage calculations: if 30% of bases are A, then 30% are T, and 40% are C and G together (20% each).
When DNA is copied, each old strand acts as a template, and complementary pairing makes sure the new strand is an accurate copy.
Pairing is specific, so the correct bases line up with each other; this is a good example of **structure being linked to function**.
core.p: The two strands of the helix are linked by **complementary base pairs**. Each base can only pair with one other base because their shapes fit together: **A always pairs with T**, and **C always pairs with G**. The pairs are held together by weak **hydrogen bonds**, two between A and T and three between C and G. Because of this rule, if you know the sequence of one strand you can always work out the other, which is the key to how DNA is copied accurately.

bullets: A sequence of **three bases** is the code for **one amino acid**.
A gene's base sequence controls the **order in which amino acids are joined** to make a specific protein.
A chain of 300 bases therefore codes for 100 amino acids (300 divided by 3).
Why three? Two bases would give only 4 x 4 = 16 combinations, too few for the 20 amino acids; three bases give 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 combinations, which is enough (extension idea).
Each protein has its own shape, determined by the order of amino acids; for example enzymes have specific active sites.
Different cells make different proteins because different genes are active, even though all body cells contain the same DNA.
core.h: Why the base order matters: the triplet code
core.p: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. Proteins are made of chains of **amino acids**, and the order of amino acids decides how the protein folds and what it does. The cell reads the gene in groups of **three bases**. Each group of three bases is a **triplet** and codes for **one amino acid**. So the base order in a gene decides the amino acid order, which decides the shape and function of the protein.

bullets: Gene to protein to characteristic: the DNA code controls the proteins, and the proteins control the features.
Alleles are different versions of the same gene; they differ in their base sequences.
Examples of proteins: enzymes (e.g. amylase), hormones (e.g. insulin), antibodies, collagen.
A change in the DNA sequence (a mutation) may change the amino acid order, so the protein may fold differently and may not work.
Not every mutation has an effect, because some do not change the protein, or change it only slightly.
This is a good link to inheritance questions about cystic fibrosis and other genetic disorders.
core.p: Proteins do most of the work in a cell: enzymes speed up reactions, hormones carry messages, antibodies fight pathogens, and structural proteins such as collagen build tissues. So genes affect an organism's characteristics by controlling which proteins are made. This connects DNA structure to inheritance and variation, because different versions of a gene (alleles) have slightly different base sequences and therefore can lead to slightly different proteins.

bullets: Non-coding regions can **control whether a gene is switched on or off**.
A **mutation** is a change in the base sequence of DNA.
Mutations occur continuously and **at random**.
A mutation inside a gene may change one or more triplets, so the **amino acid sequence** may alter.
If the order of amino acids changes, the protein may fold differently and may not work, for example an enzyme's active site may change shape so the substrate no longer fits.
A mutation in a non-coding region might change how much protein is made rather than the protein itself.
Link to evolution: if a mutation gives an advantage, natural selection can make it more common.
core.h: Non-coding DNA and mutations (Higher tier link)
core.p: Not all parts of DNA code for proteins. Some parts are **non-coding**, and some of these non-coding regions **switch genes on and off**, so variations in these regions can affect how genes are expressed (how much, or whether, a protein is made). Mutations are random changes to the DNA base sequence, and they occur continuously. Most mutations have no effect on the protein, some change it slightly, and very rarely a mutation gives a new phenotype.

bullets: Genome = **the entire genetic material of an organism**.
Every species has its own genome; closely related species have similar genomes.
The Human Genome Project was an international effort that sequenced the human genome; the first complete version was published in 2003.
Sequencing means working out the **order of the bases** along the DNA.
The genome of an individual differs slightly from other people's, which is part of why we show variation.
Genomes can also be studied for plants, animals and pathogens, for example to understand diseases or to select crops.
core.p: The **genome** of an organism is the **entire genetic material** of that organism. In humans this means all the DNA across all 23 pairs of chromosomes: roughly 3 billion base pairs, containing about 20 000 genes plus large amounts of non-coding DNA. The **whole human genome has been studied**, and its sequence was completed as part of the international Human Genome Project in 2003. Having the base sequence is the starting point for understanding what each gene does.

bullets: **Search for genes linked to different types of disease**, for example genes that increase the risk of some cancers.
**Understand and treat inherited disorders**, such as cystic fibrosis, by knowing which gene is faulty.
**Tracing human migration patterns** from the past: groups with a more recent common ancestor have more similar DNA.
Knowledge of a person's genome may allow **personalised medicine**, where drug choices suit an individual's genes.
Screening raises ethical issues, for example privacy, insurance, and whether to test embryos.
Knowing a gene is linked to disease does not mean the person will definitely get the disease; the environment also matters.
Exam tip: if a question asks 'why is it important', give a use **and** a consequence.
core.h: Importance of understanding the human genome
core.p: The spec lists three uses. First, scientists can **search for genes linked to different types of disease**, which makes it possible to screen for them. Second, understanding the genome helps us **understand and treat inherited disorders**, for example by developing tests, tailored drugs and possible gene treatments. Third, the genome is used in **tracing the migration of certain populations of humans from the past**, because small differences accumulate in DNA over generations and can be compared between groups.

bullets: Use the exact words: 'sequence of **three bases**' codes for 'one **amino acid**'.
Do not say a gene is 'a piece of protein' or that chromosomes are 'made of genes only'.
For complementary strands, go base by base: A-T, T-A, G-C, C-G.
If a question gives percentages, use A = T and C = G.
If asked about number of amino acids, divide the number of bases by 3.
Link ideas: DNA structure, protein synthesis (Higher), inheritance, mutation and evolution.
core.h: Putting it all together: exam skills
core.p: This topic is tested in short recall questions and in calculations or sequence questions. Always make sure your language matches the specification: a gene is a **small section of DNA**, a chromosome is a **long molecule of DNA with many genes**, and the genome is **all the genetic material**. When explaining, use the chain: **base order, amino acid order, protein shape, function**. Be clear about whether you are talking about a strand or the whole double helix.

exam: 1 mark 'state' questions: give the exact spec fact, e.g. 'a gene is a small section of DNA' or 'A pairs with T'.
2 mark 'describe the structure of DNA': 'two strands' + 'forming a double helix', or 'polymer of nucleotides'.
3-4 mark structure (triple): nucleotide = common sugar, phosphate and a base; alternating sugar and phosphate form the backbone; four bases A, T, C, G; complementary base pairs A-T and C-G.
Explain how a gene codes for a protein: 'the order of bases determines the order of amino acids'; 'three bases code for one amino acid'; 'the amino acids fold to give a specific shape'.
For 'importance of understanding the genome' give three uses: find genes linked to disease, understand and treat inherited disorders, trace human migration.
Complementary strand questions: write letters one by one and check each pair; copy the sequence length exactly.
Percentage questions: A = T and C = G; subtract and halve.
Number-of-amino-acids questions: divide bases by 3 (or multiply amino acids by 3 for bases).
Command words: 'state' = brief fact, 'describe' = what it is like, 'explain' = give a reason using 'because/so'.
Higher tier: link mutation to a changed amino acid sequence, a changed protein shape and a protein that no longer works.
If you see a diagram of a DNA strand, label with the specific term such as 'phosphate', 'sugar' or 'base', not just 'part'.

mistakes.r: A chromosome is a long molecule of DNA carrying many genes; a gene is a small section of DNA that codes for one protein.
mistakes.w: A gene is the same as a chromosome.

mistakes.r: A gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein; the protein then affects the characteristic.
mistakes.w: A gene codes for a characteristic.

mistakes.r: A sequence of three bases (a triplet) codes for one amino acid.
mistakes.w: Three bases code for a protein.

mistakes.r: A pairs with T and C pairs with G.
mistakes.w: A pairs with C and G pairs with T.

mistakes.r: Complementary bases are held by weak hydrogen bonds.
mistakes.w: The bases are joined to each other by strong covalent bonds across the helix.

mistakes.r: The genome is the entire genetic material of an organism, including non-coding DNA.
mistakes.w: The genome is all the genes.

mistakes.r: The code is in the order of the bases; the backbone is the same throughout.
mistakes.w: The sugar-phosphate backbone carries the code.

mistakes.r: DNA contains adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine only.
DNA is a polymer of nucleotides; proteins are polymers of amino acids.

summary: You need to describe DNA as a polymer made of two strands forming a double helix, know that a gene is a small section of DNA which codes for a particular sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein, and define the genome. Separate-science students must also describe nucleotide structure, the four bases and complementary base pairing, and explain the importance of understanding the human genome. It matters because the base order is the information that controls how every organism develops and works.

terms.d: A polymer made of two strands forming a double helix; the genetic material of cells.
A long molecule made of many repeating smaller units joined together.
The repeating unit of DNA, made of a common sugar, a phosphate group and one base.
The shape of DNA: two strands twisted around each other like a spiral ladder.
One of four chemicals in DNA: A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine), G (guanine).
A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G, between the two strands.
A weak bond that holds complementary bases together between the two strands.
The alternating sugar and phosphate groups that form the outside of each DNA strand.
A long coiled molecule of DNA in the nucleus, carrying many genes.
A small section of DNA that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.
A sequence of three bases that codes for one amino acid.
A small molecule that is the monomer of proteins; the order of amino acids decides the protein's shape.
The entire genetic material of an organism.
A change in the base sequence of DNA.
Parts of DNA that do not code for proteins; some of it switches genes on and off.
Working out the order of the bases in a piece of DNA.

worked.q: One strand of DNA has the base sequence ATGCCGTA. Write the sequence of the complementary strand. (2 marks)
steps: Pair each base in turn using A-T and C-G.
A gives T; T gives A; G gives C; C gives G; C gives G; G gives C; T gives A; A gives T.

worked.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 28% adenine. Calculate the percentage of cytosine. (3 marks)
steps: A pairs with T so thymine is also 28%.

worked.q: A gene has 150 bases in its coding sequence. How many amino acids does it code for? (1 mark)
steps: Three bases code for one amino acid.
